docs.title: Fundamental muon physics
docs.text: The muon is one of the sharpest tools we have for testing the laws of nature. We know its properties so precisely that even a tiny mismatch between measurement and theory would point to new particles or forces. This chapter covers the three big questions muon physicists ask: how strong is the muon's magnet, is its charge perfectly centred, and can it ever turn into an electron?

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › A spinning charge is a magnet
docs.text: The muon has spin and electric charge, so it behaves like a tiny bar magnet. The strength of that magnet is its magnetic moment, written μ = g (e/2m) S. The number g, the g-factor, tells us how much magnetism the muon carries for a given amount of spin. In 1928 Paul Dirac's relativistic quantum theory predicted that for a point-like particle such as the electron or muon, g should be exactly 2. Placed in a magnetic field, the muon's spin wobbles around the field direction like a spinning top — it precesses. The precession rate is set by g, so measuring how fast the spin turns is a way of measuring the muon's magnetism.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › Why g is not exactly 2
docs.text: Quantum physics says empty space is never truly empty. The muon is constantly surrounded by a fizz of virtual particles that pop in and out of existence — photons, electrons, W and Z bosons, quarks and gluons, the Higgs boson. Each one nudges the muon's magnetism very slightly. The total nudge is called the anomalous magnetic moment, a μ = (g−2)/2, and it is about 0.00116592 — a shift of roughly one part in a thousand. Physicists draw these effects as Feynman diagrams with loops. The largest contribution comes from quantum electrodynamics (QED), first calculated by Julian Schwinger in 1948 as α/2π. Smaller pieces come from the weak force and from the strong force acting on virtual quarks — the “hadronic” contributions, which are the hardest part to calculate. Here is why the muon matters more than the electron.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › Why g is not exactly 2
docs.text: The influence of a heavy, unknown particle on a μ grows with the square of the lepton's mass. The muon is 207 times heavier than the electron, so it is about 43,000 times more sensitive to such particles. If something new exists in the vacuum, the muon is far more likely to feel it.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › How g−2 is measured
docs.text: Spin-polarised muons are injected into a storage ring 14 metres across, with an extremely uniform 1.45-tesla magnetic field. As they circle, their spins turn slightly faster than their direction of motion; the difference, ω a , is directly proportional to a μ . Because a muon's decay positron is emitted preferentially along its spin, detectors around the ring see the number of high-energy positrons rise and fall — the famous “wiggle plot”. Meanwhile hundreds of NMR probes map the magnetic field to tens of parts per billion. Running at a “magic” momentum of 3.094 GeV/c cancels the effect of the focusing electric fields on the spin.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › Sixty years of measurement
docs.text: CERN (1959–1979): three generations of experiments established the storage-ring method and the magic momentum. Brookhaven E821 (1997–2004): reached 0.54 parts per million and found a value higher than the Standard Model prediction of the time. Fermilab E989 (2017–2023 running): the same ring, moved 5,000 km by barge and road, published results in 2021, 2023 and its final result in 2025 — 127 parts per billion, the most precise measurement of its kind. Our group contributed to the analysis of the precession frequency and the beam-dynamics corrections. J-PARC E34 (in preparation): a completely different approach using ultra-cold, re-accelerated muons in a compact 66-cm ring without electric focusing — an independent check with different systematics. For two decades the measurement and the theory disagreed, raising hopes of new physics.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › Sixty years of measurement
docs.text: Since 2020, new lattice-QCD calculations of the hadronic contribution have moved the prediction closer to experiment, while earlier data-driven estimates did not. Resolving that difference within the theory community is now as important as the measurement itself. Either way, the 127-ppb result places some of the strongest constraints on new particles that interact with muons. The 2025 final result →

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › A tiny lopsidedness
docs.text: An electric dipole moment (EDM) would mean the muon's charge is very slightly displaced along its spin axis — a little more “plus” at one end than the other. Spin is like an arrow that flips under time reversal, while an EDM does not, so a non-zero EDM would break time-reversal symmetry (T) and, through the CPT theorem, charge-parity symmetry (CP). Why does that matter? The Big Bang should have made equal amounts of matter and antimatter, yet our universe is made almost entirely of matter. Andrei Sakharov showed in 1967 that explaining this requires extra CP violation — far more than the Standard Model contains. The Standard Model predicts a muon EDM so small (below about 10 −38 e·cm) that any measurable signal would be unambiguous evidence of new physics.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › The frozen-spin technique at PSI
docs.text: In a magnetic field an EDM makes the spin tilt slightly up or down, but the much larger g−2 precession normally hides it. The muEDM experiment at the Paul Scherrer Institute applies a carefully tuned radial electric field that exactly cancels the g−2 precession — the spin is “frozen” along the muon's direction of motion. Any EDM then makes the spin creep steadily out of the orbit plane, and the decay positrons start to prefer “up” over “down”. Muons are stored in a compact solenoid rather than a large ring. The best direct limit today comes from the Fermilab Muon g−2 experiment, which in 2026 found |d μ | < 1.1 × 10 −19 e·cm (95% confidence), improving on Brookhaven's earlier limit. Read the news → The muEDM experiment aims to reach about 6 × 10 −23 e·cm — more than three orders of magnitude better.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › The frozen-spin technique at PSI
docs.text: Our group develops the fast muon-entrance trigger detector that tells the experiment exactly when to switch on the magnetic kick that captures each muon, and works on positron tracking.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › Can a muon become an electron? Lepton flavour violation
docs.text: Leptons come in three “flavours”: electron, muon and tau, each with its own neutrino. For decades it looked as if each flavour was separately conserved. Then neutrino oscillations showed that neutrinos do change flavour. Surprisingly, with only the neutrino masses added, the Standard Model still predicts that a charged muon turning directly into an electron is fantastically rare — around 10 −54 , far beyond any experiment. That makes these searches extraordinarily clean: a single genuine event would mean new physics. Physicists write this as non-conservation of the separate lepton numbers L e , L μ and L τ , while the total L = L e + L μ + L τ may still be conserved. Many theories of new physics — supersymmetry, extra Higgs bosons, leptoquarks — predict rates within experimental reach.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › The golden channels
docs.text: These experiments need enormous numbers of muons — up to 10 8 –10 10 per second — and detectors that can pick out one signal among trillions of ordinary decays. That demand is one of the main motivations for building new, more intense muon sources, including the SHINE muon source our group is developing.

docs.title: Fundamental muon physics › More precision physics with muons
docs.text: The muon lifetime and the weak force. Measuring how long muons live (the MuLan experiment reached 1 part per million) gives the Fermi constant G F , the most precise measure of the weak force's strength. Muonic atoms and the proton's size. A muon orbiting a proton sits 200 times closer than an electron, making it highly sensitive to the proton's size. Laser spectroscopy of muonic hydrogen at PSI in 2010 found a proton radius about 4% smaller than earlier values — the “proton radius puzzle” that reshaped atomic physics. Decay parameters. The energy and angle spectrum of the decay electron (the Michel parameters) test the V−A structure of the weak force first established with muons in 1957.

docs.title: 缪子基础物理
docs.text: 缪子是检验自然规律最锐利的工具之一。我们对它的性质了解得如此精确，以至于测量与理论之间哪怕极其微小的偏差，都可能指向新的粒子或相互作用。本章介绍缪子物理学家追问的三个大问题：缪子这枚“小磁针”有多强？它的电荷分布是否完全对称？它有没有可能直接变成电子？

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 旋转的电荷就是磁铁
docs.text: 缪子带有自旋和电荷，因此表现得像一枚微小的条形磁铁，其强弱用磁矩 μ = g (e/2m) S 来描述。数值 g（朗德g因子）告诉我们：每单位自旋对应多少磁性。1928年，狄拉克的相对论量子理论预言：对于电子、缪子这样的点粒子，g 应恰好等于2。 在磁场中，缪子的自旋会像陀螺一样绕磁场方向摆动，即“进动”。进动的快慢由 g 决定，因此测量自旋转动的速度，就能测出缪子的磁性。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 为什么 g 不恰好等于2
docs.text: 量子物理告诉我们，真空从不真正“空”。缪子周围始终环绕着不断涌现又湮灭的虚粒子——光子、电子、W和Z玻色子、夸克与胶子、希格斯玻色子……每一种都会让缪子的磁性发生极其细微的改变。这些贡献的总和称为反常磁矩 a μ = (g−2)/2，约为0.00116592，即约千分之一的偏移。 物理学家用带圈的费曼图来描述这些效应。最大的贡献来自量子电动力学（QED），施温格（Julian Schwinger）于1948年首次算出其主项 α/2π。较小的部分来自弱相互作用，以及强相互作用作用于虚夸克所产生的“强子贡献”——后者是理论计算中最困难的部分。 这正是缪子比电子更重要的原因：未知重粒子对反常磁矩的影响与轻子质量的平方成正比。缪子比电子重207倍，因此对这类粒子的敏感度高出约43000倍。如果真空中存在新东西，缪子更有可能“感觉”到它。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 如何测量 g−2
docs.text: 将自旋极化的缪子注入直径14米、磁场高度均匀（1.45特斯拉）的储存环。缪子回旋时，其自旋转动比运动方向转动稍快，二者之差 ω a 与 a μ 成正比。由于缪子衰变产生的正电子倾向于沿自旋方向发射，环周的探测器会看到高能正电子计数周期性起伏——这就是著名的“摆动图”。与此同时，数百个核磁共振探头以十亿分之几十的精度绘制磁场分布。选择3.094 GeV/c 的“魔数动量”，可以消除聚焦电场对自旋的影响。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 六十年的测量历程
docs.text: CERN（1959—1979）： 三代实验奠定了储存环方法与魔数动量技术。 布鲁克海文 E821（1997—2004）： 精度达百万分之0.54，所得数值高于当时的标准模型预言。 费米实验室 E989（2017—2023年取数）： 同一个储存环经水路和公路辗转5000公里运抵费米实验室，于2021、2023年发布结果，并于2025年发布最终结果——精度十亿分之127，是同类测量中最精确的。本课题组参与了进动频率分析和束流动力学修正。 J-PARC E34（筹备中）： 采用完全不同的方法：将超冷缪子再加速后注入直径66厘米的紧凑储存环，无需电场聚焦——系统误差完全不同的独立检验。 二十年来，实验与理论之间的差异一直让人期待新物理。2020年以来，强子贡献的格点QCD新计算使理论预言向实验值靠拢，而此前基于实验数据的估算则并非如此。弄清这两种理论方法之间的分歧，如今与测量本身同样重要。无论结果如何，十亿分之127的精度都对与缪子相互作用的新粒子给出了最强的限制之一。 2025年最终结果 →

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 微小的“偏心”
docs.text: 电偶极矩（EDM）意味着缪子的电荷沿自旋轴有极其微小的偏移——一端略“正”，另一端略“负”。自旋就像一个在时间反演下会翻转的箭头，而电偶极矩不会翻转；因此非零的电偶极矩将破坏时间反演对称性（T），并通过CPT定理破坏电荷—宇称联合对称性（CP）。 这为何重要？宇宙大爆炸理应产生等量的物质与反物质，但如今的宇宙几乎完全由物质构成。萨哈罗夫（Andrei Sakharov）在1967年指出，解释这一现象需要额外的CP破坏——远多于标准模型所包含的。标准模型预言的缪子电偶极矩极小（约10 −38 e·cm 以下），因此任何可测量的信号都将是新物理的确凿证据。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › PSI的“冻结自旋”技术
docs.text: 在磁场中，电偶极矩会使自旋略微向上或向下倾斜，但这一效应通常被大得多的 g−2 进动所掩盖。PSI（保罗·谢勒研究所）的 muEDM 实验施加一个精确调节的径向电场，恰好抵消 g−2 进动，使自旋“冻结”在缪子的运动方向上。此时若存在电偶极矩，自旋会持续缓慢地偏离轨道平面，衰变正电子便会出现“向上多于向下”的不对称。缪子储存在紧凑的螺线管中，而不是大型储存环。 目前最好的直接上限来自费米实验室 Muon g−2 实验：2026年给出 |d μ | < 1.1 × 10 −19 e·cm（95%置信度），优于此前布鲁克海文的结果。 阅读新闻 → muEDM实验的目标是达到约 6 × 10 −23 e·cm——提高三个数量级以上。本课题组研制快速缪子入射触发探测器，精确告知实验何时启动磁“踢”以俘获每个缪子，并参与正电子径迹探测研究。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 缪子能变成电子吗？带电轻子味破坏
docs.text: 轻子有三种“味”：电子、缪子和陶子，各自配有对应的中微子。几十年来，人们以为每种味都是单独守恒的。后来中微子振荡表明中微子确实会改变味。令人惊讶的是，即使在标准模型中加入中微子质量，带电缪子直接变成电子的概率仍然极低——约10 −54 ，远超任何实验的能力。这使得此类寻找极其“干净”：哪怕只发现一个真实事例，也意味着新物理。 物理学家将其表述为：各味轻子数 L e 、L μ 、L τ 分别不守恒，而总轻子数 L = L e + L μ + L τ 仍可能守恒。超对称、额外希格斯粒子、轻夸克等许多新物理理论预言的过程概率都在实验可及范围内。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › “黄金”通道
docs.text: 这些实验需要海量缪子——每秒高达10 8 —10 10 个——以及能从数万亿个普通衰变中挑出一个信号的探测器。这一需求正是建设新一代高强度缪子源（包括本课题组正在研发的SHINE缪子源）的主要动机之一。

docs.title: 缪子基础物理 › 更多缪子精密物理
docs.text: 缪子寿命与弱相互作用。 精确测量缪子寿命（MuLan 实验精度达百万分之一）可以得到费米常数 G F ——弱相互作用强度最精确的量度。 缪子原子与质子大小。 绕质子运行的缪子比电子近200倍，对质子大小极为敏感。2010年PSI对缪子氢的激光光谱测量得出的质子半径比此前数值小约4%——这一“质子半径之谜”深刻影响了原子物理研究。 衰变参数。 衰变电子的能谱与角分布（Michel参数）检验了弱相互作用的 V−A 结构——这一结构最早在1957年通过缪子确立。

docs.title: Muon sources
docs.text: To study muons you first need muons — lots of them, and ideally in a neat beam with the right energy and spin. Nature gives us a free but gentle supply from the sky. Accelerators give us beams billions of times more intense. This chapter explains where muons come from, how laboratories make them, and why the world is building a new generation of muon sources, including one in Shanghai.

docs.title: Muon sources › How muons are made
docs.text: Almost every muon, natural or artificial, starts as a pion. When a high-energy proton or photon hits an atomic nucleus, it can create pions (π + , π − ) and sometimes kaons. A charged pion lives only 26 nanoseconds and decays almost always into a muon and a neutrino: π + → μ + ν μ . Because the weak force breaks mirror symmetry, the muon comes out with its spin locked to its direction of motion — it is fully polarised, which is exactly what precision experiments need.

docs.title: Muon sources › Cosmic muons: a free gift from the sky
docs.text: Cosmic rays — mostly protons accelerated by supernova remnants and other astrophysical engines — strike the upper atmosphere and create showers of pions, which decay into muons 10–20 km above the ground. These muons reach sea level with a rate of about one per square centimetre per minute and an average energy of a few GeV. They arrive mostly from overhead: the rate falls roughly as cos²θ away from vertical, because slanted muons cross more air. Strengths: free, everywhere, and penetrating enough to cross hundreds of metres of rock — perfect for muography and for teaching. Limitations: the rate is low, the energy and direction cannot be chosen, and the spin is not under control, so precision experiments need accelerators.

docs.title: Muon sources › Accelerator muons: beams made to order
docs.text: At a muon facility, a powerful proton beam — typically a few hundred MeV to a few GeV — hits a target of graphite. The pions produced are collected by magnets, and their decay muons are steered down beamlines to experiments. By choosing how the muons are captured, physicists get very different beams.

docs.title: Muon sources › Surface muons
docs.text: Positive pions that stop just inside the target surface decay at rest, giving μ + with a fixed energy of 4.1 MeV (momentum 29.8 MeV/c) and nearly 100% spin polarisation. These low-energy muons stop within a fraction of a millimetre of material, which makes them the workhorse of materials research with muon spin rotation (μSR) and of experiments such as MEG and muEDM.

docs.title: Muon sources › Decay muons and negative muons
docs.text: Pions that fly out of the target can be guided through a long superconducting solenoid where they decay in flight. This gives higher-energy muons of either charge. Negative muons are needed for muonic atoms, element analysis and muon-catalysed fusion, since only μ − can be captured by a nucleus.

docs.title: Muon sources › Continuous or pulsed?
docs.text: Continuous beams (PSI in Switzerland, TRIUMF in Canada) deliver muons one at a time at very high average rates. Experiments can tag each muon individually — ideal for rare-decay searches and for μSR with excellent time resolution. Pulsed beams (ISIS in the UK, J-PARC in Japan, and the planned facility at CSNS in China) deliver intense bunches many times per second. Each bunch contains many muons, which suits measurements of slow processes and long time windows, and keeps backgrounds low between pulses. The most intense continuous muon beams today, at PSI, deliver up to a few hundred million surface muons per second; PSI's HIMB upgrade aims for ten billion. At the other extreme, CERN's M2 beamline provides muons of up to 160 GeV for nuclear-structure and dark-sector experiments, and Fermilab's Muon Campus serves the g−2 and Mu2e experiments.

docs.title: Muon sources › Slowing and cooling muons
docs.text: Many experiments want muons that are slower or more tightly bunched than a target naturally produces. Cooling a muon beam is hard because muons live only 2.2 μs, so it must happen fast. Low-energy muons: surface muons slowed in a thin layer of frozen noble gas emerge with only a few keV, letting scientists study thin films and interfaces nanometres below a surface. Ultra-cold muons: muons are turned into muonium, which is then laser-ionised to release almost motionless μ + that can be re-accelerated into a near-perfect beam — the technique behind J-PARC's g−2/EDM experiment. Ionisation cooling: muons pass through absorbers that remove momentum in all directions and are then re-accelerated forward. The MICE experiment in the UK demonstrated the principle in 2020 — a key step towards a future muon collider.

docs.title: Muon sources › A new idea: muons from electrons
docs.text: Most muon sources use proton accelerators. An alternative is to use a high-energy electron beam. When electrons hit a thick target, they radiate high-energy photons (bremsstrahlung); those photons can then create pions, or directly make muon–antimuon pairs. Electron linacs can also run at very high repetition rates, giving a fine time structure that proton machines struggle to match. Shanghai's SHINE facility is an 8 GeV superconducting electron linac built for a hard X-ray free-electron laser, with a pulse rate of up to about a million per second. Our group is designing China's first electron-driven muon source downstream of its beam dump, turning the spent electron beam into a new muon facility for particle physics, materials science and muography.

docs.title: 缪子源
docs.text: 要研究缪子，首先得有缪子——数量要多，最好还是能量合适、自旋整齐的束流。大自然从天空免费为我们提供了温和的缪子来源；加速器则能产生强度高出数十亿倍的缪子束。本章介绍缪子从哪里来、实验室如何制造缪子，以及为什么世界各地——包括上海——正在建设新一代缪子源。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 缪子是如何产生的
docs.text: 几乎每一个缪子——无论天然还是人工——最初都来自π介子。高能质子或光子撞击原子核时，会产生π介子（π + 、π − ），有时还有K介子。带电π介子的寿命只有26纳秒，几乎总是衰变为一个缪子和一个中微子：π + → μ + ν μ 。由于弱相互作用破坏宇称，产生的缪子自旋与运动方向锁定——即完全极化，这正是精密实验所需要的。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 宇宙线缪子：来自天空的免费礼物
docs.text: 宇宙线——主要是被超新星遗迹等天体“加速器”加速的质子——撞击高层大气，产生π介子簇射，π介子在离地10—20公里处衰变为缪子。这些缪子以约每分钟每平方厘米1个的通量到达海平面，平均能量为几个GeV。它们主要从头顶方向而来：偏离竖直方向时通量大致按 cos²θ 减小，因为斜射的缪子要穿过更多空气。 优点： 免费、无处不在，穿透力强，可穿越数百米岩石——非常适合缪子成像和教学。 局限： 通量低，能量和方向无法选择，自旋也不受控制，因此精密实验必须依靠加速器。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 加速器缪子：“定制”的束流
docs.text: 在缪子装置中，高功率质子束（能量通常为几百MeV至几GeV）轰击石墨靶。产生的π介子被磁铁收集，其衰变产生的缪子沿束线被输送到各实验终端。通过选择不同的收集方式，可以得到性质迥异的缪子束。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 表面缪子
docs.text: 在靶表面附近停止的正π介子发生静止衰变，产生能量固定为4.1 MeV（动量29.8 MeV/c）、自旋极化接近100%的 μ + 。这种低能缪子在材料中不到一毫米就会停下，因此成为缪子自旋旋转（μSR）材料研究以及 MEG、muEDM 等实验的主力束流。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 衰变缪子与负缪子
docs.text: 飞出靶的π介子可以在长超导螺线管中飞行衰变，从而得到两种电荷、能量更高的缪子。负缪子是缪子原子、元素分析和缪子催化核聚变所必需的，因为只有 μ − 才能被原子核俘获。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 连续束还是脉冲束？
docs.text: 连续束 （瑞士PSI、加拿大TRIUMF）以极高的平均流强逐个提供缪子，实验可单独标记每个缪子——非常适合稀有衰变寻找以及时间分辨率优异的μSR测量。 脉冲束 （英国ISIS、日本J-PARC以及中国散裂中子源规划中的装置）每秒提供多次高强度脉冲，每个脉冲包含大量缪子，适合测量慢过程和长时间窗口，且脉冲间本底很低。 目前最强的连续缪子束位于PSI，每秒可提供数亿个表面缪子；PSI的HIMB升级计划目标为每秒一百亿个。另一方面，CERN 的 M2 束线可提供能量高达160 GeV的缪子，用于核子结构和暗物质相关实验；费米实验室的“缪子园区”则服务于 g−2 和 Mu2e 实验。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 让缪子“慢下来、冷下来”
docs.text: 许多实验需要比靶自然产生的更慢、更集中的缪子。由于缪子只能存活2.2微秒，冷却必须在极短时间内完成，难度很大。 低能缪子： 表面缪子穿过一薄层固态惰性气体后，能量降至几keV，可用于研究表面以下几纳米处的薄膜与界面。 超冷缪子： 先将缪子变成缪子素，再用激光电离，释放出几乎静止的 μ + ，随后再加速成近乎完美的束流——这是 J-PARC g−2/EDM 实验的关键技术。 电离冷却： 缪子穿过吸收体，在各方向上损失动量，随后只在前进方向上被重新加速。英国MICE实验于2020年验证了这一原理——这是迈向未来缪子对撞机的关键一步。

docs.title: 缪子源 › 新思路：用电子产生缪子
docs.text: 大多数缪子源使用质子加速器，另一种方案是利用高能电子束。电子打在厚靶上会辐射高能光子（轫致辐射），这些光子可以产生π介子，或直接产生缪子—反缪子对。电子直线加速器还能以极高的重复频率运行，提供质子加速器难以实现的精细时间结构。 上海SHINE装置是为硬X射线自由电子激光建设的8 GeV超导电子直线加速器，脉冲重复频率可达每秒约一百万次。本课题组正在其束流垃圾桶下游设计中国首个电子驱动缪子源，把“用过”的电子束变成服务于粒子物理、材料科学与缪子成像的新型缪子装置。

docs.title: Muon detection techniques
docs.text: Muons are invisible, silent and gone in microseconds — so how do we know they are there? Every muon detector relies on the same idea: as a fast charged particle passes through matter, it knocks electrons off atoms and leaves a trail of energy behind. Turn that trail into light or an electrical pulse, and you can count muons, time them, track them and even read their spin.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › How muons leave a trace
docs.text: Ionisation. A typical cosmic muon loses about 2 MeV for every centimetre of water it crosses (the Bethe–Bloch formula describes this precisely). It is a “minimum-ionising particle”: it deposits little energy, so it travels a long way — through metres of rock. Multiple scattering. Each nucleus it passes gives the muon a tiny sideways kick. Dense, high-atomic-number materials like lead or uranium kick harder — the basis of scattering muography. Decay. A muon that stops in a detector decays after about 2.2 μs, emitting an electron or positron whose direction reveals the muon's spin. Cherenkov light. A muon moving faster than light travels in water (about 75% of c) emits a cone of blue light — an optical “sonic boom”.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › Scintillators: turning muons into flashes of light
docs.text: A scintillator is a material — often a plastic doped with fluorescent molecules, or an inorganic crystal — that gives off a short flash of light when a charged particle passes through it. A photodetector turns the flash into an electrical pulse: traditionally a photomultiplier tube (PMT), and increasingly a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM), a fingernail-sized chip that works at low voltage and in magnetic fields. Scintillators respond within nanoseconds, are robust and cheap, and can be cut into bars, tiles or thin fibres. That is why they are everywhere: in desktop CosmicWatch counters, in the muon trigger our group builds for muEDM, and in our muography systems — the Cosmic-ray Muography System uses layers of triangular scintillator bars read out by SiPMs, and the SciFi-MST design uses scintillating fibres.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › Scintillators: turning muons into flashes of light
docs.text: Inorganic crystals such as lead fluoride (PbF 2 ) or lutetium-based crystals are dense and measure particle energies: the Muon g−2 experiment uses 1,296 PbF 2 crystals read by SiPMs to measure every decay positron.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › Gaseous detectors: following the track
docs.text: In a gaseous detector, the electrons knocked free by a muon drift towards thin wires or fine meshes held at high voltage. Near the wire the electric field is so strong that each electron triggers an avalanche of thousands more, producing a measurable signal. Knowing which wire fired and when tells us where the muon passed. Geiger counters — the classic “click” detector, simple but without position information. Multi-wire proportional and drift chambers — invented by Georges Charpak (Nobel Prize 1992), they made electronic particle tracking possible. Micro-pattern detectors — Micromegas, GEMs and resistive plate chambers (RPCs) give sub-millimetre position resolution over large areas at modest cost, ideal for large muography panels. Time projection chambers — record a full 3D picture of each track in a large gas volume.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › Silicon detectors: the finest detail
docs.text: Thin silicon sensors divided into strips or millions of pixels locate a particle to a few micrometres. For low-energy muon decays, every gram of material scatters the electrons, so the Mu3e experiment at PSI uses pixel sensors thinned to just 50 micrometres — thinner than a human hair — cooled by gaseous helium.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › Cherenkov detectors: seeing the cone
docs.text: Huge tanks of ultra-pure water lined with photomultipliers catch the ring of Cherenkov light a muon makes. The size, sharpness and orientation of the ring reveal the particle's direction and type. Giant neutrino observatories such as Super-Kamiokande in Japan, and IceCube buried in Antarctic ice, identify muons this way — muons produced by neutrinos are one of their main signals.

docs.title: Muon detection techniques › Nuclear emulsion: photographic film for particles
docs.text: Nuclear emulsion is a thick photographic film. A passing charged particle leaves a line of silver grains that appears after development. Emulsion captured the decay of a pion into a muon in 1947 and helped clarify the muon's identity. Today, automated microscopes scan emulsion films at high speed with sub-micrometre precision. Because the films need no power and are light and portable, they were used by the ScanPyramids team to discover the hidden void in the Great Pyramid.

docs.title: 缪子探测技术
docs.text: 缪子看不见、听不到，几微秒就消失了——我们怎么知道它们存在？所有缪子探测器都基于同一个原理：高速带电粒子穿过物质时会把原子中的电子打出来，沿途留下能量的“足迹”。把这条足迹转化为光或电脉冲，就能对缪子计数、计时、追踪其径迹，甚至读出它的自旋。

docs.title: 缪子探测技术 › 缪子如何留下痕迹
docs.text: 电离。 典型的宇宙线缪子每穿过1厘米水约损失2 MeV能量（贝特—布洛赫公式可精确描述）。它是“最小电离粒子”：沉积的能量很少，因此能走得很远——穿透数米岩石。 多次散射。 经过的每个原子核都会给缪子一个微小的侧向偏折。铅、铀等高密度、高原子序数的材料偏折更强——这正是散射型缪子成像的基础。 衰变。 停在探测器中的缪子约2.2微秒后衰变，发射出的电子或正电子的方向能揭示缪子的自旋。 切伦科夫光。 当缪子在水中的速度超过光在水中的速度（约光速的75%）时，会发出一个蓝色光锥——光学上的“音爆”。

docs.title: 缪子探测技术 › 闪烁体：把缪子变成闪光
docs.text: 闪烁体是一种材料——通常是掺有荧光分子的塑料或无机晶体——带电粒子穿过时会发出短暂的闪光。光电探测器把闪光转换为电脉冲：传统上用光电倍增管（PMT），如今越来越多地使用硅光电倍增管（SiPM）——一种指甲大小的芯片，工作电压低，且能在磁场中工作。 闪烁体响应时间为纳秒量级，坚固且成本低，可切割成条、块或细光纤，因此应用极其广泛：桌面式 CosmicWatch 计数器、本课题组为 muEDM 研制的缪子触发探测器，以及我们的缪子成像系统——宇宙线缪子成像系统（CMS）采用由SiPM读出的三角形闪烁体条， SciFi-MST 方案则采用闪烁光纤。 氟化铅（PbF 2 ）、镥基晶体等无机晶体密度高，可测量粒子能量：Muon g−2 实验使用1296块由SiPM读出的 PbF 2 晶体来测量每一个衰变正电子。

docs.title: 缪子探测技术 › 气体探测器：追踪径迹
docs.text: 在气体探测器中，被缪子电离出的电子向加有高电压的细丝或细网漂移。在丝附近，电场强到每个电子都能引发数千个电子的“雪崩”，形成可测量的信号。根据哪根丝在何时响应，就能确定缪子经过的位置。 盖革计数器 ——经典的“咔哒”探测器，结构简单，但不给出位置信息。 多丝正比室与漂移室 ——由夏帕克（Georges Charpak，1992年诺贝尔物理学奖）发明，使粒子径迹的电子学测量成为可能。 微结构气体探测器 ——Micromegas、GEM 和阻性板室（RPC）能以适中成本在大面积上实现亚毫米位置分辨，非常适合大型缪子成像探测面板。 时间投影室 ——在大体积气体中记录每条径迹的完整三维图像。

docs.title: 缪子探测技术 › 硅探测器：最精细的细节
docs.text: 分割成微条或数百万像素的薄硅传感器，可将粒子位置确定到几微米。对于低能缪子衰变，每一克材料都会散射电子，因此PSI的 Mu3e 实验使用仅50微米厚（比头发还细）的像素传感器，并用氦气冷却。

docs.title: 缪子探测技术 › 切伦科夫探测器：看见光锥
docs.text: 装满超纯水、内壁布满光电倍增管的巨大水箱，可以捕获缪子产生的切伦科夫光环。光环的大小、清晰度和方向揭示了粒子的方向与种类。日本超级神冈、南极冰层中的 IceCube 等大型中微子观测站正是这样识别缪子——由中微子产生的缪子是它们的主要信号之一。

docs.title: 缪子探测技术 › 核乳胶：粒子的“照相底片”
docs.text: 核乳胶是一种厚的照相胶片，带电粒子穿过后会留下一串银颗粒，冲洗后即可看到。1947年，核乳胶记录下了π介子衰变为缪子的过程，帮助人们认清了缪子的身份。如今，自动化显微镜能以亚微米精度高速扫描乳胶片。由于乳胶片无需供电、轻便易携带，ScanPyramids 团队就用它发现了大金字塔中的隐藏空腔。

docs.title: Applications of muons
docs.text: Muons are not only for testing the laws of physics. Fired into a material, a muon becomes a tiny spy that reports on magnetism deep inside. Captured by an atom, it makes the atom sing a characteristic X-ray note. Bound into a molecule, it can even make nuclei fuse. This chapter tours the practical uses of muons, from quantum materials and batteries to Roman coins and asteroid dust.

docs.title: Applications of muons › A compass needle inside the material
docs.text: μSR stands for muon spin rotation, relaxation and resonance. A beam of fully spin-polarised positive muons is fired into a sample, where each muon stops at a site between the atoms. If there is a local magnetic field there, the muon's spin precesses around it like a compass needle swinging. About 2.2 μs later the muon decays, and its positron flies off preferentially along the spin direction. By recording millions of these positrons with detectors around the sample, scientists reconstruct how the spins turned — and so measure the magnetic fields, and how they fluctuate, at the atomic scale. What makes μSR special is that it needs no external probe field, works in any kind of sample — crystals, powders, thin films, even liquids — including in zero applied field, and is sensitive to very weak and very fast-changing magnetism that other techniques miss.

docs.title: Applications of muons › What μSR is used for
docs.text: Superconductors: measuring how deep magnetic fields penetrate (the penetration depth) and whether a superconductor breaks time-reversal symmetry — key clues to how unconventional superconductors work. Quantum magnets: detecting tiny ordered moments and slow spin fluctuations in frustrated magnets and candidate quantum spin liquids. Energy materials: watching lithium and sodium ions hop through battery electrodes, and hydrogen diffuse in storage materials. Semiconductors: a muon can grab an electron to form muonium, which mimics an isolated hydrogen atom — the most important and hardest-to-study impurity in semiconductors. Soft matter and chemistry: following radicals and molecular dynamics in polymers, liquids and biological molecules.

docs.title: Applications of muons › What μSR is used for
docs.text: Two examples from recent research: Time-reversal symmetry breaking in Sr 2 RuO 4 , a long-debated unconventional superconductor, studied under uniaxial strain. Quasi-static and dynamic spins in NaYbSe 2 , a candidate quantum spin liquid on a triangular lattice.

docs.title: Applications of muons › An atom's X-ray fingerprint
docs.text: When a negative muon is slowed down in a material, an atom captures it in a high orbit. The muon then cascades down to the lowest orbit in less than a nanosecond, emitting X-rays at each step. Because the muon is 207 times heavier than an electron, these “muonic X-rays” are about 200 times more energetic than ordinary X-rays — tens of keV up to several MeV — and their energies are a unique fingerprint of the element. Non-destructive: the high-energy X-rays escape even from deep inside an object, so nothing has to be cut or sampled. All elements at once: light elements such as carbon, nitrogen and oxygen can be measured alongside heavy metals. Depth profiling: the muon's momentum sets how deep it stops, so scientists can scan from micrometres to centimetres below the surface.

docs.title: Applications of muons › An atom's X-ray fingerprint
docs.text: MIXE has been used to study silver Roman coins and bronze artefacts without damaging them, to analyse meteorites, and to measure the composition of tiny grains returned from asteroid Ryugu by the Hayabusa2 mission. It is also used to check lithium distribution inside working batteries.

docs.title: Applications of muons › Muon-catalysed fusion (μCF)
docs.text: Nuclear fusion normally needs temperatures of a hundred million degrees, so that nuclei collide hard enough to overcome their electric repulsion. A muon offers a different route. If a negative muon replaces the electron in a molecule of deuterium and tritium, the molecule shrinks about 200 times and the two nuclei sit so close together that they fuse within about a picosecond — at room temperature. The muon is usually released and can catalyse another fusion. History: predicted by Andrei Sakharov and Charles Frank in the late 1940s, and first seen by Luis Alvarez's group in a hydrogen bubble chamber in 1956. The catch: one muon can catalyse roughly 100–150 fusions before it decays or sticks to a helium nucleus (“α-sticking”). Making a muon costs more energy than those fusions release, so μCF is not yet a power source.

docs.title: Applications of muons › Muon-catalysed fusion (μCF)
docs.text: Today: research focuses on increasing the number of cycles per muon, new reaction mechanisms, and using μCF as a compact source of fusion neutrons or slow muons.

docs.title: Applications of muons › Other uses
docs.text: Muography — imaging pyramids, volcanoes, tunnels and cargo with cosmic muons. See the Muography Applications chapter. Reliability of electronics — as chips shrink, a single cosmic muon can flip a bit in memory. Muon beams are used to test how often this happens. Cosmic-ray monitoring — networks of muon detectors track changes in the cosmic-ray flux caused by solar activity and the atmosphere.

docs.title: 缪子的应用
docs.text: 缪子并不只用于检验物理定律。射入材料后，缪子就成了一名微型“侦察兵”，报告材料深处的磁性信息；被原子俘获后，它会让原子“唱”出特征X射线；结合进分子中，它甚至能促使原子核发生聚变。本章将带你了解缪子的实际用途——从量子材料、电池，到古罗马钱币和小行星尘埃。

docs.title: 缪子的应用 › 放进材料内部的指南针
docs.text: μSR 是缪子自旋旋转、弛豫与共振的统称。将完全自旋极化的正缪子束射入样品，每个缪子会停在原子之间的某个位置。若该处存在局部磁场，缪子自旋就会像指南针摆动一样绕磁场进动。约2.2微秒后缪子衰变，其正电子倾向于沿自旋方向飞出。通过样品周围的探测器记录数百万个正电子，科学家就能重建自旋的转动过程，从而在原子尺度上测量磁场及其涨落。 μSR 的独特之处在于：无需外加探测场，适用于任何材料——晶体、粉末、液体，甚至零磁场环境——并且对其他技术难以探测的极弱、极快变化的磁性高度敏感。

docs.title: 缪子的应用 › μSR 的应用
docs.text: 超导体： 测量磁场穿透深度，以及超导体是否破坏时间反演对称性——这是理解非常规超导机制的关键线索。 量子磁体： 探测阻挫磁体和量子自旋液体候选材料中极微弱的有序磁矩与缓慢的自旋涨落。 能源材料： 观察锂、钠离子在电池电极中的跳跃，以及氢在储氢材料中的扩散。 半导体： 缪子可以俘获电子形成缪子素，模拟孤立的氢原子——这是半导体中最重要却最难研究的杂质。 软物质与化学： 追踪聚合物、液体和生物分子中的自由基与分子动力学过程。 两个近期研究实例： Sr 2 RuO 4 中的时间反演对称性破缺 ——在单轴应力下研究这一长期存在争议的非常规超导体。 NaYbSe 2 中的准静态与动态自旋 ——一种三角晶格量子自旋液体候选材料。

docs.title: 缪子的应用 › 原子的X射线“指纹”
docs.text: 负缪子在材料中慢化后，会被原子俘获到高能级轨道上，随后在不到一纳秒的时间内逐级跃迁到最低轨道，每一步都发射X射线。由于缪子比电子重207倍，这些“缪子X射线”的能量比普通X射线高约200倍——从几十keV到几MeV——其能量是元素独一无二的“指纹”。 无损： 高能X射线即使从物体深处也能逃逸出来，因此无需切割或取样。 多元素同时分析： 碳、氮、氧等轻元素可以与重金属同时测量。 深度剖析： 缪子的动量决定其停止深度，因此可以从表面以下几微米到几厘米逐层扫描。 MIXE 已被用于在不损坏的前提下研究古罗马银币和青铜器、分析陨石，以及测定“隼鸟2号”从小行星“龙宫”带回的微小颗粒成分，还可用于检测工作中电池内部的锂分布。

docs.title: 缪子的应用 › 缪子催化核聚变（μCF）
docs.text: 核聚变通常需要上亿摄氏度的高温，才能让原子核以足够大的能量碰撞、克服彼此之间的电排斥。缪子提供了另一条途径：如果用负缪子替换氘—氚分子中的电子，分子会缩小约200倍，两个原子核靠得极近，在约一皮秒内就会发生聚变——而且是在室温下。缪子通常会被释放出来，继续催化下一次聚变。 历史： 20世纪40年代末由萨哈罗夫与弗兰克（Charles Frank）预言，1956年由阿尔瓦雷茨团队在氢气泡室中首次观测到。 瓶颈： 一个缪子在衰变或“粘附”到氦核上（α粘附）之前，大约能催化100—150次聚变。而产生一个缪子所消耗的能量多于这些聚变释放的能量，因此μCF目前还不能作为能源。 现状： 研究重点包括提高每个缪子的催化次数、探索新的反应机制，以及将μCF用作紧凑的聚变中子源或慢缪子源。

docs.title: 缪子的应用 › 其他应用
docs.text: 缪子成像 ——利用宇宙线缪子对金字塔、火山、隧道和货物进行成像，详见 缪子成像应用 一章。 电子器件可靠性 ——随着芯片尺寸不断缩小，单个宇宙线缪子就可能导致存储器比特翻转。缪子束被用来测试这类“软错误”的发生频率。 宇宙线监测 ——缪子探测器网络可以追踪太阳活动和大气变化引起的宇宙线通量变化。

docs.title: Muography applications
docs.text: Muography is X-ray imaging on a giant scale. Instead of an X-ray tube, it uses the cosmic muons that fall on every part of the Earth, day and night, for free. Because muons can pass through hundreds of metres of rock, they let us look inside pyramids, volcanoes, tunnels and shipping containers — without drilling, digging or adding any radiation.

docs.title: Muography applications › Muon radiography: counting the shadow
docs.text: Muons lose energy steadily as they pass through matter (described by the Bethe–Bloch formula). The more material along a path, the fewer muons have enough energy to make it through. A detector placed below or beside an object counts muons arriving from each direction and compares the count with what it would see under open sky. Knowing the cosmic-muon energy spectrum, the missing fraction tells us how much material — the density times the length — lies along each line of sight. Works for very large objects — mountains, volcanoes, pyramids, dams — from tens of metres to kilometres. Gives a 2D density map from one location; combining several viewpoints gives a 3D picture, much like a CT scan. Hidden voids show up as directions with more muons than expected; dense bodies show up as fewer.

docs.title: Muography applications › Muon scattering tomography: measuring the kicks
docs.text: For smaller objects, a few metres across, almost all muons pass straight through — but not quite straight. Each muon is deflected by many tiny scatterings off atomic nuclei, and the deflection is much larger in dense, high-atomic-number materials such as lead, uranium or steel. Tracking detectors above and below the object measure each muon's incoming and outgoing direction; the scattering angle reveals what it passed through. The spread (root-mean-square) of scattering angles grows with the amount of material, measured in radiation lengths, and falls with muon momentum. A simple, widely used 3D algorithm, the Point of Closest Approach (PoCA), assigns each scatter to the point where the incoming and outgoing tracks come closest. More advanced methods use maximum-likelihood or machine learning.

docs.title: Muography applications › Muon scattering tomography: measuring the kicks
docs.text: Ideal for finding high-Z material in cargo, inspecting nuclear waste containers, or locating steel reinforcement and defects in concrete. Try it yourself: our SciFi-MST live demo simulates a scintillating-fibre muon scattering tomograph in your browser, reconstructing scattering-density slices event by event.

docs.title: Muography applications › Geophysics: inside volcanoes and mountains
docs.text: Since the 2000s, Japanese teams led by Hiroyuki Tanaka have imaged the magma conduits of volcanoes such as Asama and Satsuma-Iwojima, and watched them change before eruptions. Similar work has followed at Vesuvius, Stromboli and Etna in Italy and La Soufrière in the Caribbean. Muography is also used to map ore bodies and caverns in mines, and karst cavities in limestone.

docs.title: Muography applications › Archaeology: hidden rooms
docs.text: In 1970 Luis Alvarez placed spark chambers in a chamber beneath the Pyramid of Khafre and showed that there were no large hidden rooms in the region they covered. Almost fifty years later, in 2017, the ScanPyramids team combined nuclear emulsion, scintillator and gas detectors to find a large void above the Grand Gallery of the Great Pyramid of Khufu, and in 2023 confirmed a hidden corridor behind its north face. Muography has also been used beneath Naples to map ancient underground cavities, and to look for anomalies inside the historic city wall of Xi'an in China.

docs.title: Muography applications › Safety and security
docs.text: After the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi accident, muography was used to see where melted nuclear fuel had ended up inside the damaged reactors, where no person or camera could go. Scattering systems scan trucks and shipping containers for hidden nuclear material, and inspect sealed casks of spent nuclear fuel.

docs.title: Muography applications › Cities and infrastructure
docs.text: Modern cities depend on what lies beneath them — tunnels, metro lines, utility corridors and foundations. Muography can check for voids, water ingress and sediment without interrupting traffic, and can be left in place to monitor changes over months. Engineers are also testing it on blast furnaces, dams, bridges and the ground above underground construction.

docs.title: Muography applications › Muography in our group
docs.text: Our group began working on muography in mid-2024, bringing detector and simulation know-how from the Muon g−2 and muEDM experiments to problems in Shanghai and beyond. Shanghai Outer Ring Tunnel: a pilot run inside this immersed tunnel beneath the Huangpu River showed that the muon flux tracks the tidal water level, demonstrating muography's sensitivity to the sediment overburden ( J. Appl. Phys. 2025). Cosmic-ray Muography System: a three-layer scintillator-bar tracker at TDLI, now taking radiography data. Field survey in Malaysia (2026): our portable detectors were taken abroad for the first time, to an air-raid shelter, a limestone cave and other sites in karst regions where underground cavities can cause road collapses. Challenge Cup 2026: the project “Muon imaging — safeguarding the development of megacities” won a First Prize in the Shanghai entrepreneurship competition.

docs.title: 缪子成像应用
docs.text: 缪子成像是一种“超大尺度”的X光成像。它不需要X光管，而是利用昼夜不停、免费落在地球每个角落的宇宙线缪子。由于缪子能穿透数百米厚的岩石，我们得以“看见”金字塔、火山、隧道和集装箱的内部——无需钻孔、开挖，也不增加任何辐射。

docs.title: 缪子成像应用 › 缪子透射成像：数“影子”
docs.text: 缪子穿过物质时会持续损失能量（由贝特—布洛赫公式描述）。路径上的物质越多，能穿过去的缪子就越少。将探测器放在物体下方或侧面，统计来自各个方向的缪子数，并与空旷天空下的计数相比较；已知宇宙线缪子能谱，缺失的比例就能告诉我们每条视线上有多少物质——即密度与长度的乘积。 适用于超大型物体——山体、火山、金字塔、大坝——尺寸从几十米到几公里。 单一位置可得到二维密度图；结合多个观测位置可重建三维图像，类似CT扫描。 隐藏的空腔表现为缪子比预期多的方向；致密物体则表现为缪子更少。

docs.title: 缪子成像应用 › 缪子散射成像：测量“偏折”
docs.text: 对于尺寸只有几米的较小物体，几乎所有缪子都能穿过——但并非笔直穿过。每个缪子都会因与原子核的大量微小散射而偏折，且在铅、铀、钢铁等高密度、高原子序数材料中偏折更大。在物体上方和下方放置径迹探测器，测量每个缪子的入射与出射方向，散射角就能揭示它穿过了什么。 散射角分布的展宽（均方根）随物质的辐射长度数增加而增大，随缪子动量增大而减小。 一种简单而广泛使用的三维重建算法是“最近点法”（PoCA），把每次散射归于入射与出射径迹最接近的点；更先进的方法采用最大似然或机器学习。 非常适合在货物中寻找高原子序数物质、检查核废料容器，或定位混凝土中的钢筋与缺陷。 亲自体验：我们的 SciFi-MST 在线演示 在浏览器中模拟闪烁光纤缪子散射成像仪，逐个事例重建散射密度切片。

docs.title: 缪子成像应用 › 地球物理：火山与山体内部
docs.text: 21世纪以来，田中宏幸（Hiroyuki Tanaka）领导的日本团队对浅间山、萨摩硫黄岛等火山的岩浆通道进行了成像，并观测到喷发前的变化。意大利的维苏威、斯特龙博利、埃特纳火山以及加勒比海的苏弗里耶尔火山也开展了类似研究。缪子成像还被用于勘测矿山中的矿体与洞穴，以及石灰岩中的岩溶空洞。

docs.title: 缪子成像应用 › 考古：隐藏的空间
docs.text: 1970年，阿尔瓦雷茨在哈夫拉金字塔下方的墓室中放置火花室，证明在其覆盖范围内不存在大型隐藏墓室。近五十年后的2017年，ScanPyramids 团队综合使用核乳胶、闪烁体和气体探测器，在胡夫大金字塔大走廊上方发现了一个巨大空腔，并于2023年证实其北立面后方存在一条隐藏通道。缪子成像还被用于绘制那不勒斯地下古代洞穴，以及探测中国西安古城墙内部的异常结构。

docs.title: 缪子成像应用 › 安全与安保
docs.text: 2011年福岛第一核电站事故后，缪子成像被用来查明熔化的核燃料在受损反应堆内的位置——那里人和摄像机都无法进入。散射成像系统可以扫描卡车和集装箱中隐藏的核材料，并检查密封的乏燃料容器。

docs.title: 缪子成像应用 › 城市与基础设施
docs.text: 现代城市依赖其脚下的一切——隧道、地铁、综合管廊和地基。缪子成像可以在不中断交通的情况下检测空洞、渗水和泥沙淤积，并可长期放置，持续数月监测变化。工程师们还在高炉、大坝、桥梁以及地下施工区域上方的地层中测试这项技术。

docs.title: Muonium
docs.text: Take a hydrogen atom and replace its proton with a positive muon. You get muonium — an atom with no nucleus in the usual sense, made only of two leptons. It lives just 2.2 microseconds, yet it is one of the cleanest systems in all of physics for testing quantum theory, matter–antimatter symmetry and even how antimatter falls under gravity.

docs.title: Muonium › What is muonium?
docs.text: Muonium (chemical symbol Mu) is a bound state of a positive muon μ + and an electron e − . It was discovered in 1960 by Vernon Hughes and colleagues, who saw the characteristic precession of muonium's spin in argon gas. Because the muon is still 207 times heavier than the electron, muonium has almost the same size and chemistry as hydrogen. Chemists treat it as a very light hydrogen isotope, and use it to study how hydrogen atoms react, tunnel and bind — especially in semiconductors, where isolated hydrogen is hard to observe directly. Muonium is made by stopping a beam of positive muons in a material where they can pick up an electron. In silica powder or laser-drilled silica aerogel, some muonium atoms diffuse out of the surface into vacuum, where they can be studied free of any surrounding material. A newer approach produces a cold muonium beam from superfluid helium.

docs.title: Muonium › A perfect test of quantum electrodynamics
docs.text: Hydrogen is the textbook atom, but its proton is a messy object made of quarks and gluons, and its size limits how precisely theory can predict hydrogen's energy levels. Muonium has no such problem: both the muon and electron are, as far as we know, point-like. Its energy levels can be calculated almost entirely from quantum electrodynamics (QED), so comparing theory and experiment is an exceptionally clean test. Ground-state hyperfine splitting (about 4.463 GHz): the energy difference between the muon and electron spins being parallel or opposite. Measured to 12 parts per billion at Los Alamos in 1999; it gives the muon's mass and magnetic moment, an essential input to the Muon g−2 experiment. The MuSEUM experiment at J-PARC aims to improve it further. 1S–2S transition : measured by two-photon laser spectroscopy, it determines the ratio of the electron and muon masses.

docs.title: Muonium › A perfect test of quantum electrodynamics
docs.text: The Mu-MASS project at PSI aims to improve it by about a thousand times. Lamb shift : a tiny splitting of the n = 2 levels caused by vacuum fluctuations, recently measured in muonium at PSI.

docs.title: Muonium › Matter–antimatter symmetry (CPT)
docs.text: The CPT theorem says that the laws of physics are unchanged if you swap particles for antiparticles, mirror space and reverse time together. Comparing the 1S–2S transition of muonium with that of antimuonium (μ − e + ), or measuring muonium's energy levels as the Earth rotates, can reveal tiny violations of CPT or Lorentz symmetry.

docs.title: Muonium › Can muonium turn into antimuonium?
docs.text: In muonium-to-antimuonium conversion, μ + e − spontaneously becomes μ − e + . This changes the muon number and the electron number each by two units — a form of charged lepton flavour violation that is forbidden in the Standard Model, but predicted by several theories with doubly charged Higgs bosons or heavy neutral leptons. Current limit: the MACS experiment at PSI (1999) found the conversion probability is below 8.3 × 10 −11 (90% confidence). MACE: the proposed Muonium-to-Antimuonium Conversion Experiment in China aims to be sensitive to probabilities around 10 −13 — about a hundred times better. It would detect the energetic electron from the μ − decay together with the slow positron left behind.

docs.title: Muonium › Does antimatter fall down? Muonium and gravity
docs.text: Almost everything we know about gravity comes from ordinary matter. Muonium offers a rare chance to test gravity on antimatter — its mass is dominated by the antimuon μ + — and on a particle from the second generation. Because muonium contains no quarks, it tests gravity on purely leptonic matter. One approach searches for an annual modulation of muonium's 1S–2S frequency as the Earth's distance from the Sun changes. Another sends a high-quality beam of muonium through a Mach–Zehnder atom interferometer and measures how much it falls in a few microseconds — a drop of only around a tenth of a nanometre, smaller than an atom, which demands extraordinary precision. This idea, proposed by K. Kirch and K. S. Khaw in 2014, is being pursued by the LEMING collaboration at PSI.

docs.title: 缪子素
docs.text: 把氢原子中的质子换成正缪子，就得到了缪子素——一种没有通常意义上原子核、仅由两个轻子组成的原子。它只能存活2.2微秒，却是物理学中检验量子理论、物质—反物质对称性，乃至反物质如何在引力下“下落”的最纯净体系之一。

docs.title: 缪子素 › 什么是缪子素？
docs.text: 缪子素（化学符号 Mu）是正缪子 μ + 与电子 e − 的束缚态。1960年，休斯（Vernon Hughes）及其同事在氩气中观测到缪子素自旋的特征进动，从而发现了它。 由于缪子仍比电子重207倍，缪子素的大小和化学性质几乎与氢相同。化学家把它当作一种极轻的氢同位素，用来研究氢原子如何反应、隧穿和成键——在孤立氢原子难以直接观测的半导体中尤其有用。 将正缪子束停在能让它们俘获电子的材料中，即可产生缪子素。在二氧化硅粉末或激光打孔的二氧化硅气凝胶中，部分缪子素会从表面扩散到真空中，从而可以在不受周围物质影响的情况下进行研究。一种较新的方法则是利用超流氦产生冷缪子素束。

docs.title: 缪子素 › 量子电动力学的完美检验
docs.text: 氢是教科书中的标准原子，但其质子是由夸克和胶子构成的复杂对象，质子的大小限制了理论预言氢原子能级的精度。缪子素没有这个问题：就目前所知，缪子和电子都是点粒子，其能级几乎完全可以由量子电动力学（QED）计算，因此理论与实验的比较格外纯净。 基态超精细分裂 （约4.463 GHz）：缪子与电子自旋平行与反平行时的能量差。1999年在洛斯阿拉莫斯测量精度达十亿分之12；它给出了缪子的质量和磁矩，是 Muon g−2 实验的重要输入量。J-PARC 的 MuSEUM 实验正致力于进一步提高精度。 1S—2S 跃迁 ：通过双光子激光光谱测量，可确定电子与缪子的质量比。PSI 的 Mu-MASS 项目目标是将精度提高约一千倍。 兰姆位移 ：由真空涨落引起的 n = 2 能级的微小分裂，近期已在PSI对缪子素进行了测量。

docs.title: 缪子素 › 物质—反物质对称性（CPT）
docs.text: CPT定理指出：同时交换粒子与反粒子、镜像翻转空间并反转时间，物理规律保持不变。比较缪子素与反缪子素（μ − e + ）的 1S—2S 跃迁，或随地球自转测量缪子素能级，可以揭示CPT或洛伦兹对称性的微小破缺。

docs.title: 缪子素 › 缪子素能变成反缪子素吗？
docs.text: 在缪子素—反缪子素转换中，μ + e − 自发变为 μ − e + 。这一过程使缪子数和电子数各改变两个单位——是一种被标准模型禁戒的带电轻子味破坏，但若干包含双电荷希格斯粒子或重中性轻子的理论预言它可能发生。 现有上限： PSI的MACS实验（1999年）给出转换概率小于 8.3 × 10 −11 （90%置信度）。 MACE： 中国提出的缪子素—反缪子素转换实验（MACE）目标灵敏度约为 10 −13 ——提高约一百倍。它将同时探测 μ − 衰变产生的高能电子以及残留的慢正电子。

docs.title: 缪子素 › 反物质会“往下掉”吗？缪子素与引力
docs.text: 我们对引力的认识几乎全部来自普通物质。缪子素提供了一个难得的机会，用以检验引力对反物质的作用——它的质量主要来自反缪子 μ + ——同时也检验引力对第二代粒子的作用。由于缪子素不含夸克，它检验的是纯轻子物质所受的引力。 一种方法是寻找缪子素 1S—2S 频率随地日距离变化而出现的年度调制。 另一种方法是让高品质缪子素束穿过马赫—曾德尔原子干涉仪，测量它在几微秒内下落的距离——仅约十分之一纳米，比一个原子还小，需要极高的精度。这一方案由 K. Kirch 与 K. S. Khaw（许金祥）于2014年提出，目前PSI的 LEMING 合作组正在推进。

docs.title: Muon g-2 sets the tightest direct limit on the muon electric dipole moment
docs.text: One year after its final measurement of the muon magnetic anomaly, the Muon g-2 Collaboration at Fermilab has reported a new search for a different property of the muon: its electric dipole moment (EDM). An EDM would mean a tiny, permanent separation of positive and negative charge inside the muon. Because it violates time-reversal and charge-parity (CP) symmetry, the Standard Model predicts a value of about 10 −38 e ·cm, far below any experimental reach. Seeing a non-zero muon EDM would therefore be an unambiguous sign of new physics, and a possible new source of the CP violation needed to explain why the universe is made of matter. The experiment searches for the EDM almost for free, using the same data as the g-2 analysis. The magnetic moment drives the familiar horizontal precession of the muon spin; an EDM would tilt the precession plane and add a small vertical oscillation to the decay positrons. The straw-tracker stations measured the average vertical angle of these positrons, using data from Runs 2 and 3 (2019–2020), about a quarter of the full Fermilab dataset. No EDM was found. docs.title: Our muEDM muon trigger detector paper is out in EPJC
docs.text: Our paper “Construction and characterization of a muon trigger detector for the PSI muEDM experiment” has been accepted in The European Physical Journal C (86, 911, 2026). 📄 Read the paper (preprint: arXiv:2603.27483 ). The first author is our PhD student Guan Ming Wong. The muEDM experiment at PSI will search for the muon’s electric dipole moment with the frozen-spin technique. Muons entering the storage solenoid must be identified within about 140 ns so that a pulsed magnetic kicker can be fired in time. The upgraded trigger uses a 0.1 mm-thin gate scintillator and a thicker active-aperture scintillator, read out by SiPMs: a muon that hits the gate but not the aperture generates the trigger in under 10 ns. The detector was characterised with 22.5 MeV/c positive muons at PSI’s πE1 beamline, and a Geant4 simulation reproduced the measured event topologies to about 97%. The results show the detector is ready for the Phase-1 setup of the experiment. This work builds on the prototype reported earlier in Radiation Detection Technology and Methods , and was carried out with colleagues from PSI and the University of Pisa.

docs.title: Muon g-2 Collaboration wins the 2026 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics
docs.text: The 2026 Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics has been awarded to the Muon g-2 Collaborations — three generations of experiments at CERN, Brookhaven National Laboratory and Fermilab — for decades of pioneering work pushing the limits of measurement precision. The US3 million prize is shared among 376 researchers, including members of the Shanghai Jiao Tong University muon physics team, one of the core contributing groups. The final Fermilab result, released in 2025, determined the muon's anomalous magnetic moment to 127 parts per billion — the most precise measurement to date and about 30,000 times more precise than CERN's first experiment in 1965. Because the muon g-2 is sensitive to new particles and interactions, this measurement remains one of the most stringent tests of the Standard Model. docs.title: Cosmic-ray Muography System (CMS) Now Online and Begins First Muon Radiography Measurements at TDLI
docs.text: The Cosmic-ray Muography System (CMS), developed by the TDLI Muon Physics Group, is now online and has begun taking data in radiography mode. The system consists of three tracking layers, each built from 1.5 cm-wide triangular scintillator bars read out by SiPMs, covering an active area of approximately 50 cm × 50 cm. Combined with CAEN’s A5202 front-end electronics, the CMS provides a compact, modular, high-resolution platform for muon imaging. A series of commissioning measurements was carried out at three locations within TDLI: two inside Tianwen Hall and one on the B1 underground level. The preliminary results are promising: the cosmic-ray muon flux in the 90° < φ < 180° range at Location #3 (B1) is significantly lower than at the two surface-level sites. This reduction reflects muons traversing the denser structural material above the underground site, demonstrating the detector’s sensitivity and confirming that it operates properly. These first measurements are a significant milestone in establishing the CMS as the first functional muography instrument in Shanghai, paving the way for future structural, geological, and subsurface imaging studies around the city.

docs.title: Fast Muon Trigger System Prototype Readied for PSI’s muEDM Experiment
docs.text: Two new studies mark key milestones toward the world’s most sensitive search for the muon electric dipole moment. The PSI muEDM experiment aims to probe physics beyond the Standard Model by improving the sensitivity to the muon’s electric dipole moment (EDM) to 6 × 10⁻²³ e·cm—four orders of magnitude beyond the current limit. docs.title: Final results from the Muon g-2 experiment at Fermilab
docs.text: The Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment announced its final results at 11:00 PM Beijing time on June 3. The new measurement agrees closely with the results published in 2021 and 2023 and reaches an unprecedented precision of 127 parts per billion (ppb), surpassing the original goal of 140 ppb. It is the most precise measurement of the muon anomalous magnetic moment to date. Although recent theoretical calculations have weakened the hints of new physics in the muon g-2, the high-precision experimental result still places strong constraints on extensions of the Standard Model. The Shanghai Jiao Tong University team played a key role in measuring the muon spin precession frequency and the associated beam dynamics corrections. Within our group at TDLI, PhD student Yonghao Zeng performed an independent analysis of the anomalous precession frequency, using Gaussian Process Regression to model beam dynamics effects. Postdoctoral researchers Siew Yan Hoh and Yusuke Takeuchi contributed to the beam dynamics corrections, including the pitch and differential decay corrections. The result has been published in Physical Review Letters 135, 101802 (2025) and is also available on arXiv: https://arxiv.or

It was a very fruitful trip: he learned about the latest developments in the field, picked up practical knowledge on detector development and scientific outreach, and, more importantly, reconnected with old friends. For more details, please visit the event’s webpage: https://indico.cern.ch/event/1291157/overview .

docs.title: Exhibition at the Shanghai Natural History Museum
docs.text: Our group recently took part in an exhibition showcasing science and technology (S&T) innovations from Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU). The exhibition was specially arranged to celebrate the partnership between SJTU and the Shanghai Tech Museum in promoting S&T innovation and public outreach. We took this opportunity to present our newly developed muography detector, with a live LED event display board, to the public; it attracted much attention, especially from younger visitors. We hope to promote this technique for imaging the city’s underground structures to help prevent disasters. Jun Kai, Tianqi, Yingying, and Siew Yan explained the detector to visitors at the museum on July 11–12. Yonghao, Tianqi, Xingyun, Jun Kai, Guan Ming, Ning, Yusuke, and Siew Yan were involved in developing the detector. The original announcement can be found here: https://mp.weixin.qq.com/s/ax8_iFvnaPjBfQ0VuUYr_A .

docs.title: Jun Kai NG successfully defends his Master’s thesis
docs.text: Jun Kai NG (黄俊凯) successfully defended his Master’s thesis, “Validation of the Calorimeter Acceptance Model in the Fermilab Muon g-2 Experiment”, on 12 May 2024. The whole team congratulates him! He has been awarded the CSC PhD Scholarship (2024–2028) and will stay in our group as a PhD student, working on the SHINE Muon Source project.

docs.title: Yimin Wan and Xingyun Huang have successfully defended their Bachelor’s theses
docs.text: Yimin Wan (万一民) and Xingyun Huang (黄幸运) successfully defended their Bachelor’s theses on 4 June 2024. They worked on “Design and Construction of Spark Chamber Frame Structure, Gas System, and Camera System” and “Spark-Chamber-based Muon Mass Measurement”. The whole team congratulates them! Xingyun will stay in our group as a PhD student working on the PSI muEDM project, and Yimin will join the Shanghai Advanced Research Institute (SARI) as a Master’s student in Microelectronics and Solid-State Electronics.

docs.title: Workshop on Muon Physics at the Intensity and Precision Frontiers (MIP2024)
docs.text: Our group recently participated in the MIP2024 workshop at Peking University, Beijing, on April 20–21, 2024. Kim Siang chaired the precision measurement session, while three group members (Yusuke, Siew Yan, and Guan Ming) gave plenary talks and nine presented posters. Fangchao, Jun Kai, and Yuzhi won Best Poster Awards for their work on the Shanghai Muon Source, the Muon g-2 experiment, and the muEDM experiment, respectively. Congratulations to them! For more information about the workshop, please visit https://indico.cern.ch/event/1356341/ . The next edition, MIP2025, will be hosted by Hunan University in Changsha, and we are all looking forward to it!

docs.title: SHINE电子束流科学应用与关键技术研讨会
docs.text: Our group recently participated in the Workshop on Scientific Applications and Key Technologies of the SHINE Electron Beam (SHINE电子束流科学应用与关键技术研讨会) on April 1–2. Kim Siang gave a talk on the SHINE-based muon source and its applications. Several other TDLI members also attended, and we enjoyed a comprehensive tour of the SHINE facility. We are all very excited about the progress of SHINE’s construction!

docs.title: Lanzhou Trip for Muon Physics Exchange
docs.text: On March 3–4, Kim Siang visited Lanzhou for the first time for an academic exchange on muography with Prof. Zhiyi Liu’s group, accompanied by several officials from the Shanghai government. He also gave a seminar on muon physics at the Institute of Modern Physics (IMP), CAS. We enjoyed a comprehensive and truly eye-opening tour of IMP’s accelerator facility. The trip was a great success: we learned a great deal about muography from Prof. Liu’s group and had extensive discussions about future collaborations with both Lanzhou University and IMP. We look forward to our next visit!

docs.title: SJTU Summer Research Internship Program 2024
docs.text: We are accepting students for the SJTU Summer Research Internship this summer! Our project is the measurement of muon properties using tabletop setups in our laboratory at the Tsung-Dao Lee Institute. Eligibility requirements: – Applicants must have completed at least one year of an undergraduate program and be currently enrolled as undergraduates; – Applicants must hold a GPA of at least 3.0 on a 4.0 scale, or equivalent; – Applicants from non-English-speaking countries must provide an English language proficiency certificate. The program runs from July 1 to August 11, 2024. Applications must be submitted by May 30 to be considered. More information about the internship can be found in this brochure: https://global.sjtu.edu.cn/en/news/view/718.

docs.title: 上海市和教育部重点实验室2023年度学术委员会联席会议
docs.text: Kim Siang represented the accelerator-based particle physics experimental group in the annual report to the Key Laboratory of Shanghai and the MOE. In his presentation, he described the group’s progress in its three main directions: collider experiments (ATLAS and CEPC), the fixed-target experiment (Dark SHINE), and storage ring experiments (Muon g-2 and muEDM). Much progress was made in 2023, and we hope for more in 2024!

docs.title: 27th J-PARC Muon g-2/EDM collaboration meeting at Niigata University
docs.text: Meng attended the 27th J-PARC Muon g-2/EDM Collaboration Meeting at Niigata University and gave a talk on the status of the muon polarization monitor. Exchanges between the Shanghai Muon Physics Group and the KEK/J-PARC muon physics group have become a regular occurrence, and we look forward to an even stronger collaboration in the future!

docs.title: 2023年粒子物理与核物理上海研讨会
docs.text: Kim Siang and Tianqi gave talks on the Shanghai Muon Source and the PSI muEDM experiment at the Shanghai Particle and Nuclear Physics Annual Meeting, held at Tongji University. It was a great opportunity to present the progress of our research program and to meet fellow physicists from the region.

docs.title: 《致交论道》Dec 2023
docs.text: Kim Siang was invited to speak at the 《致交论道》 event organized by Zhiyuan College, SJTU. The topic of discussion was “What is the new physics behind the N-th decimal place?”

docs.title: ICFA Seminar 2023
docs.text: Kim Siang was recently invited to give an overview talk on electromagnetic dipole moments at the ICFA Seminar 2023 on “Future Perspectives in High-Energy Physics”, held at DESY in Hamburg from November 27 to December 1, 2023. The seminar is an international exchange of information focusing on plans for future facilities in particle physics. Attendance is by invitation only, and participants include the directors of most of the world’s major laboratories in the field, senior particle and accelerator physicists, and government science officials from several countries. Please visit the link for more details about the meeting: https://indico.desy.de/event/38293/ .

docs.title: MELODY 2023
docs.text: Our group recently participated in the first Workshop on Muon Science Technology and Industry (MELODY 2023), held from 3 to 6 November 2023 at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS). Kim Siang presented our group’s work on the Shanghai Muon Source, the Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment, and the PSI muEDM experiment. None of this progress would have been possible without the hard work of all our group members! More information about the workshop can be found here: https://indico.ihep.ac.cn/event/20601/ .

docs.title: Faculty-student exchange session at the Zhiyuan Innovative Research Center (ZIRC) 2024
docs.text: On Oct 25, 2023, Kim-Siang presented a poster on “Precise measurements of muon properties and muon factory” at the faculty-student exchange session (2024年“致远学者研究计划”师生交流会) of the Zhiyuan Innovative Research Center (ZIRC). The original report on the event can be found here: https://zhiyuan.sjtu.edu.cn/html/zhiyuan/news_view.php?id=4001 .

docs.title: The 3rd Asian-European-Institutes Workshop for BSM
docs.text: Kim Siang was invited to present the latest results of the Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment at the 3rd Asian-European-Institutes (AEI) Workshop for BSM, held from 3 to 6 October 2023 at the famous hot-spring resort of Ikaho, Gunma, Japan. More information about the workshop can be found here: https://conference-indico.kek.jp/event/234/ .

docs.title: NuFact 2023: The 24th International Workshop on Neutrinos from Accelerators
docs.text: Our group participated in the NuFact 2023 workshop at Seoul National University, giving technical talks on the Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment (Kim Siang) and the PSI muEDM experiment (Guan Ming). Jun Kai also presented a poster on the November 2022 test beam of the muEDM project. It was great to reconnect with many long-time friends from Japan, Europe, and the US. Besides the rich physics program, the organizers set aside half a day for an excursion in Seoul. We visited the famous Gyeongbokgung (the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty), the National Folk Museum of Korea (inside Gyeongbokgung), and the National Museum of Korea. The conference banquet was held at Sesangui Modeun Achim on the 50th floor of the FKI Plaza, with a great night view of Seoul. More information about the conference can be found here: http://nufact2023.snu.ac.kr/index.html .

docs.title: Muon g-2 Physics Week at Liverpool 2023
docs.text: Kim Siang attended the Muon g-2 collaboration’s Physics Week in Liverpool, his first in-person Physics Week since joining TDLI in 2019. He presented the current status of the SJTU group’s precession frequency analysis, co-organized the precession frequency analysis workshop, and gave a talk on detector acceptance at the beam dynamics workshop. All of this was made possible by the continuous contributions of Cheng, Yonghao, and Jun Kai over the past few months.

docs.title: SUT-PSI School of Muon and Neutron Physics
docs.text: From July 10 to 14, our young research team had the privilege of attending the SUT-PSI School of Muon and Neutron Physics , hosted by Suranaree University of Technology (SUT) in Thailand. The well-curated curriculum blended theoretical and practical elements, designed to stimulate intellectual curiosity and deepen our understanding of low-energy particle physics. The programme featured extensive lectures on the many roles of muons and neutrons in low-energy particle physics, along with hands-on tutorials on current practices in particle physics simulation and analysis. These were complemented by an eye-opening tour of the Synchrotron Light Research Institute, a centre of scientific progress and innovation in the region. The academic programme was well balanced with cultural immersion and networking opportunities. A memorable visit to the Phimai Historical Park let us appreciate Thailand’s rich heritage, while lively discussions with fellow physicists encouraged the exchange of ideas and sparked new perspectives. docs.title: WIN 2023: 29th International Workshop on Weak Interactions and Neutrinos
docs.text: Cheng participated in the WIN 2023 workshop at the beautiful Zhuhai Campus of Sun Yat-sen University in Guangdong Province, where he presented the current status of the Muon g-2 experiment on behalf of the collaboration. For more details, please visit the event’s webpage: https://indico.ihep.ac.cn/event/18269/ .

docs.title: 缪子束物理与应用研讨会2023
docs.text: Kim Siang took part in the Muon Beam Physics and Applications Workshop, held on June 19–20 at the newly built Huizhou campus of the Institute of Modern Physics (IMP), Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). At the workshop, he presented his concept of a High-Repetition-Rate Pulsed Muon Source based on the Shanghai Hard X-ray Free Electron Laser Facility (SHINE). Visiting the state-of-the-art IMPCAS campus and the facility under construction made the trip an enlightening and enjoyable experience.

docs.title: J-PARC Muon g-2/EDM collaboration meeting and New Physics Forum
docs.text: From June 11 to 15, our team members Tianqi Hu, Jun Kai Ng, and Yonghao Zeng made their first trip to Japan. During the visit, they took part in academic activities at KEK, J-PARC, and Ochanomizu University (including the 24th New Physics Forum on June 13), all centered on muon physics and new physics beyond the Standard Model. They also gave plenary talks in a dedicated session for visitors from Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU). Their accounts of the trip are shared below: “The J-PARC Muon g-2/EDM Collaboration Meeting brought together leading scientists from Canada, the UK, and Japan to discuss the details of muon g-2/EDM theory and experiment. The meeting served as a forum for pioneering research and new ideas in this fascinating field. As guests, we had the opportunity to tour the J-PARC experimental facility and present the PSI muon EDM experiment. The in-depth discussions on the experiment’s design and on diverse topics, including EDM theory, cosmology, and dark matter, broadened our understanding. docs.title: PPC 2023: XVI International Conference on Interactions between Particle Physics and Cosmology
docs.text: Kim Siang recently took part in the PPC 2023 conference (Jun 12 – 16), held at the Institute for Basic Science (IBS) in Daejeon, South Korea. docs.title: Poster presentation at the IPAC’23 international conference
docs.text: Meng and Jiangtao presented a poster on our Shanghai Muon Source project at the 14th International Particle Accelerator Conference (IPAC’23), held on May 7–12, 2023, in Venice, Italy. The conference, held on an island in Venice, was attended by over 1,000 participants and featured many talks, poster presentations, and social activities. docs.title: Workshop on Muon Physics at the Intensity and Precision Frontiers (MIP2023)
docs.text: The Workshop on Muon Physics at the Intensity and Precision Frontiers (MIP2023) was successfully held at our institute on April 15–16, 2023. It featured about 100 in-person participants, 25 plenary talks, and 15 poster presentations. Cheng presented the current status of the Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment, Tianqi presented the status of the PSI muon EDM experiment, and Meng presented the idea of the SHINE Muon Source. Yonghao, Jun Kai, Guan Ming, Meng, Xintong, Fangyuan, and Siyuan also presented posters on their work on the Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment, the PSI muon EDM experiment, and the J-PARC muon g-2/EDM experiment. Our PRP and graduate students (Jiangtao Wang, Meng Lv, Fangchao Liu, Liang Wang, and Siyuan Chen) won one of the three best poster awards. Congratulations! We also gave the workshop attendees a tour of our newly constructed muon lab. More information can be found at https://indico-tdli.sjtu.edu.cn/event/1465/ .

docs.title: SJTU-KEK Muon Physics Exchange on the Minhang Campus
docs.text: Prof. Tsutomu Mibe (KEK and Univ. of Tokyo) and Dr. Yusuke Takeuchi (Kyushu University) visited Shanghai on April 13–14, 2023, for the 2nd meeting (and the 1st in person) of the SJTU-KEK Muon Physics Exchange Program, supported by the NSFC and the JSPS Academic Exchange Program. We shared our recent progress in muon physics experiments and had lunch together at GIMLID Pizza on the SJTU Minhang Campus. Prof. Liang Li, Prof. Kim Siang Khaw, Guan Ming Wong, Meng Lv, Jiangtao Wang, Yonghao Zeng, and Zejia Lu joined the academic exchange lunch session.

docs.title: Muon EDM Collaboration April Meeting 2023 at PSI
docs.text: Kim Siang made his first international business trip in three years, travelling to PSI for the Muon EDM Collaboration April Meeting 2023 on April 15–16. He presented TDLI’s contribution to the collaboration: the muon telescope detector used in the November 2022 beam test. The two-day meeting was very fruitful, with plenty of physics and technical discussions, and delicious food from PSI’s OASE cafeteria.

docs.title: A PMT-based setup for measuring muon polarization
docs.text: In addition to the setup designed and built by the ZIRC team, we have another version of the muon spin polarization measurement setup, based on PMTs and plastic scintillators.

docs.title: A setup for detecting atmospheric muons
docs.text: After months of hard work by the ZIRC project team, a setup for measuring the polarization of atmospheric muons is now in operation! We look forward to extracting important information for subsequent studies of muon polarization.

docs.title: Muon Detector Lab completes renovation

docs.title: Physics of Fundamental Symmetries and Interactions – PSI2022

docs.title: SJTU-KEK Muon Physics Exchange Workshop 2022

docs.title: Zhiyuan Scholar Research Program

docs.title: Faculty-student exchange session at the Zhiyuan Innovative Research Center (ZIRC) 2022

docs.title: Recruiting 2022 PhD students at TDLI

docs.title: Virtual Workshop on Potential Fermilab Muon Campus & Storage Ring Experiments

docs.title: 1st TDLI Career Planning Session
docs.text: Kim-Siang was an invited guest at the first TDLI Career Planning Session. Drawing on his own career path as an example, he shared his perspectives on how to choose a research topic, what matters most during a PhD, and the importance of not limiting oneself in the choice of research topic or where to carry out the research.

docs.title: Chalk Talk@ZIRC No. 31 – Visiting TDLI

docs.title: Tsung-Dao Lee Frontier Lecture and Special Seminar on Muon g-2

docs.title: First Results from the Fermilab Muon g-2 Experiment
docs.text: After almost three years of analyzing the Run 1 data taken in spring 2018, our collaboration has published the first results on the muon anomalous magnetic moment (muon g-2) in a series of Physical Review papers.

docs.title: TDLI Tea Time Discussion about “Precision Measurements and Fundamental Physics”
docs.text: Kim-Siang led a discussion on “Precision Measurements and Fundamental Physics” at the Friday TDLI Tea Time of the new 2021 semester. docs.title: Dark SHINE Simulation and Analysis Workshop II

docs.title: Seminar at the 21st J-PARC muon g-2/EDM collaboration meeting

docs.title: Our first SJTU Sports Day!
docs.text: Maintaining a healthy lifestyle and taking an active part in team building are very important in one’s scientific career. There is no better way to do both than by joining the University’s Sports Day!

docs.title: NSFC Grants for Kim-Siang Khaw
docs.text: Kim-Siang Khaw has been awarded an NSFC General Program grant (面上基金) and an NSFC Research Fund for International Young Scientists grant (外国青年学者研究基金), both starting in January 2021. The grants support precision muon physics experiments on the muon anomalous magnetic moment and the muon electric dipole moment.

docs.title: Midterm evaluation for 38th PRP
docs.text: Meng Lv and Le He gave an excellent presentation on our Dark SHINE experiment at the midterm evaluation of the 38th Participation in Research Program (PRP) on November 18, 2020.

docs.title: muCool demonstrates muon-beam transverse phase-space compression
docs.text: The muCool collaboration, of which Kim-Siang has been a member since 2011, has published results demonstrating the transverse part of muon-beam phase-space compression. The paper was highlighted as an Editors’ Suggestion in Phys. Rev. Lett. and can be found at https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.125.164802 (arXiv: 2003.11986 ).

docs.title: Simulation and Analysis Workshop for the Dark SHINE Experiment
docs.text: On August 21, 2020, we successfully held a workshop on simulation and analysis for the Dark SHINE experiment. Presentations covered several aspects of the experiment, followed by a fruitful discussion of its future plans.

docs.title: Kick-off workshop for the frozen-spin muon EDM search at PSI
docs.text: On February 17, 2020, Kim-Siang presented “Overview of the muon EDM searches” at the “Kick-off workshop for the search of a muon EDM using the frozen spin technique at PSI” (17–19 February 2020). More information can be found here: https://indico.psi.ch/event/8339/ .

docs.title: 3rd workshop for “Physics at the high-intensity hadron accelerator in China”
docs.text: Kim Siang presented “Progress in Precision Muon Physics” at the 3rd Workshop on “Physics at the High-Intensity Hadron Accelerator in China”, held on 7–8 December 2019 at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) in Dongguan. More information can be found here: https://indico.ihep.ac.cn/event/10779/ .

docs.title: Faculty-student exchange session at the Zhiyuan Innovative Research Center (ZIRC)
docs.text: On Dec 4, 2019, Kim-Siang presented a poster on the Muon g-2 experiment at the faculty-student exchange session (2020年“致远学者研究计划”师生交流会) of the Zhiyuan Innovative Research Center (ZIRC).

docs.title: Workshop on “New Developments of Muon Precision Physics”
docs.text: Kim-Siang gave an update on the Fermilab Muon g-2 experiment at the workshop “New Developments of Muon Precision Physics” at KEK, Japan, held on November 27–28, 2019. More information can be found on the event page .

docs.title: Appointment of Kim-Siang Khaw
docs.text: On October 1, 2019, Kim-Siang Khaw was appointed Tsung-Dao Lee Fellow at the Tsung-Dao Lee Institute (TDLI) and Tenure-track Associate Professor at the School of Physics and Astronomy (SPA), Shanghai Jiao Tong University.
